newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan warms to idea of female monarch, poll shows.
newsitem.headline: Japan warms to idea of female monarch, poll shows.

text.p: A growing number of Japanese would accept a female monarch as head of the imperial family if Japan broke with its current rule of male-only succession, according to an opinion poll published on Thursday.

The Jiji news agency survey of 2,000 people, conducted earlier this month, said 30.3 percent supported the idea of a woman taking the Japanese throne, compared with 27.8 percent in a similar poll at the same time last year.
Those opposed to the principle of an empress heading the imperial family stood at 18.6 percent, down from 21.4 percent a year ago.
The last empress to occupy Japan's Chrysanthemum Throne was Empress Go-Sakuramachi, who reigned from 1762 to 1771.

Male succession, a tradition since the ninth century, was enshrined in the law after the 1868 Meiji Restoration which opened up Japan to Western influence. This means that the crown passes only through the male line and the role of empress is merely one of consort to the monarch.

The question of changing the law of succession to allow an empress regnant has become an issue in recent years because so far there is no male heir once Crown Prince Naruhito succeeds his father Emperor Akihito.
Naruhito and his wife Princess Masako, who married four years ago, have no children, and the heir to the throne's younger brother Prince Akishino has two daughters but no son.

Japan's tabloid press is constantly on the lookout for signs of a Masako pregnancy, going so far as to speculate over the fertility issue on the basis of whether she wears flat shoes or misses public appearances.
The Imperial Household Agency, the secretive government office that is in charge of royal affairs, has time and again denied that Masako, formerly a diplomat, is expecting a child.
